questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes Azure Machine Learning's three managed compute options from Lesson 2?
options: A compute instance is a single-owner cloud workstation for interactive work; a compute cluster is a shared, autoscaling pool of nodes that training jobs run on; serverless compute requires no compute resource to be created at all
A compute cluster is a single-owner cloud workstation; a compute instance is a shared, autoscaling pool of nodes used for jobs
Serverless compute is simply a compute cluster with max_instances set to 1
A compute instance can scale down to zero nodes when idle, while a compute cluster cannot
All three compute options bill a flat hourly rate regardless of whether a job is actually running
A compute cluster has a single owner and runs Jupyter or VS Code directly, the same as a compute instance
questions.explain: A compute instance is a managed cloud workstation with a single owner, used for interactive work. A compute cluster is a shared pool of one or more nodes that scales up for jobs and can scale down to zero when idle. Serverless compute means you create nothing at all — you submit a job without naming a compute and the service provisions capacity for you.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two roles: it's the compute instance that has a single owner and runs an interactive Jupyter/VS Code session, while the compute cluster is the shared, autoscaling pool jobs run on. Getting the two backwards is exactly the mistake to avoid.

questions.code:
env = Environment(
    name="churn-env",
    image="mcr.microsoft.com/azureml/openmpi4.1.0-ubuntu20.04",
    conda_file="environment/conda.yml",
    description="scikit-learn churn model",
)
questions.prompt: Which of the three Azure ML environment categories from Lesson 2 does this Environment definition belong to, and why?
options: System-managed, because it supplies a conda specification plus a base Docker image and lets conda build the Python environment on top
Curated, because it references a prebuilt environment by URI with no further configuration
User-managed, because it brings the entire container image with nothing left for Azure ML to build
Serverless, because no compute target is named in the definition
questions.explain: A system-managed environment supplies a conda_file plus a base Docker image, and conda builds the Python environment on top of that image. This definition does exactly that, unlike a curated environment (referenced by a registry URI with nothing else to configure) or a user-managed one (the whole container image, with no conda step at all).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the four companion Azure resources a new Azure ML workspace connects to, per Lesson 1.
options: The storage account stores artifacts such as job logs, uploaded files, and the notebooks used on compute instances
Key Vault stores secrets that compute targets and the workspace need
Application Insights collects diagnostic information from your inference endpoints
A Container Registry is created only when needed, such as for building custom environments, and a workspace can exist without one
All four companion resources must be newly created for every workspace — you can never attach ones that already exist
questions.explain: The storage account holds artifacts and notebook files; Key Vault holds secrets; Application Insights collects diagnostics from endpoints; and the Container Registry is created only when a custom environment needs one, meaning a workspace can exist without it. Microsoft's guidance is that you can bring existing resources instead of letting Azure create new ones, so the last statement is false.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on a compute instance, the argument that sets automatic shutdown after a period of inactivity is ________, and per the docs it can only be set at creation time, not changed later through the SDK.
questions.explain: idle_time_before_shutdown_minutes is the ComputeInstance argument that controls idle shutdown. Lesson 2 specifically notes you can't change the idle time on an existing instance from the SDK — you must set it at creation, which is why a forgotten running workstation is such a classic surprise bill.

questions.prompt: Match each Azure ML interface to the task it suits best, per Lesson 5.
right: Build reusable Python workflows: compose a single command into a sweep, then into a pipeline
Automation and CI/CD, with job definitions kept in git for code review
Explore the workspace, inspect metrics and logs, and do quick no-code tasks like the guided training-job form
Edit notebooks attached to a compute instance using a familiar desktop or web editor
questions.explain: Studio is best for exploring, inspecting runs, and quick no-code tasks. The SDK v2 is for building reusable Python workflows, incrementally composing a command into a sweep and then a pipeline. The CLI v2 with YAML suits automation and CI/CD, since YAML job files can be code-reviewed in git. The VS Code extension opens a notebook attached to the compute instance, kernel, and workspace file system.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of registering a versioned data asset and using it in a training job in the correct order, per Lessons 3-4.
items: Create a Data object with a name, version, type (uri_file, uri_folder, or mltable) and a path
Call ml_client.data.create_or_update(...) to register that version in the workspace
Reference the registered asset in a job's inputs as Input(type=..., path="azureml:<name>:<version>")
Submit the job with ml_client.jobs.create_or_update(job), and let the training script read the path it is handed
questions.explain: You first describe the asset (name, version, type and path), then register it, then reference that exact name and version as a job input, and finally submit the job so the script reads whatever path it is handed. Each registered version is immutable, which is exactly what makes a job that consumed it reproducible later.

questions.prompt: A data scientist needs to register a single folder containing thousands of PNG images for a training job. Which data asset type from Lesson 3 should they choose, and why?
options: uri_folder, because it is meant for a folder of files such as images or text
uri_file, because it is meant for a single file such as one CSV
mltable, because it is the format AutoML expects for any dataset
None of these — data assets can only be registered from CSV files
questions.explain: uri_folder is for a folder of files — CSV/Parquet files, or images and text — which fits a folder of thousands of PNGs. uri_file is for exactly one file, and mltable is for tabular data with a schema, not an images folder.

questions.prompt: A submitted command job shows status Preparing for several minutes and then fails before ever reaching Running. What does that most likely indicate, per Lesson 6?
options: A problem with the environment — Preparing is when the Docker image or conda environment is built, so a failure there is not your training script's fault
The training script raised an exception partway through
The compute cluster has reached its max_instances limit
The job's declared output folder could not be created
questions.explain: Preparing is specifically the stage where the service builds the Docker image or sets up the conda environment. A job that fails there failed because of the environment, not the model code — which is also why you'd look in a different place (the environment build logs) than you would for a script error.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about MLflow experiment tracking in Azure Machine Learning, per Lesson 7.
options: A run can log parameters, metrics, artifacts, and a packaged model
Inside an Azure ML job, mlflow.start_run() must be called explicitly before logging, exactly as it would on a laptop
mlflow.autolog() can report training-set metrics, such as training_accuracy_score, that look like test performance but are not
The Azure ML SDK v2 has its own built-in logging system that is preferred over MLflow
mlflow.search_runs results can be filtered with an expression such as "metrics.auc>0.8"
questions.explain: A run records parameters, metrics, artifacts and models. In an Azure ML job a run is already started for you, so there is no start_run call needed, unlike on a laptop. Autolog's training_accuracy_score and similar names are scores on training data, not held-out test data, which is why you still log test metrics yourself. The SDK v2 has no logging of its own — MLflow is the recommended tool. search_runs does support filter expressions like metrics.auc>0.8.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: because the churn dataset has only about 27% churners, Lesson 8 recommends choosing ________ as AutoML's primary metric instead of plain accuracy, since threshold-based metrics like accuracy can behave poorly under class imbalance.
questions.explain: AUC_weighted is the primary metric Lesson 8 recommends for an imbalanced classification problem like churn, where threshold-based metrics such as plain accuracy can be misleadingly high or low depending on the imbalance.

questions.prompt: An AutoML classification job is given 1,000 rows of training data, with no validation data and no fold count specified. Per Lesson 8, how does AutoML validate the model in this case?
options: By cross-validation using three folds, since the training data has 20,000 rows or fewer and at least 1,000 rows
By a 10 percent holdout split, the default for any dataset size
By ten-fold cross-validation, since any dataset under 20,000 rows always gets ten folds
It raises an error and requires validation_data to be supplied explicitly
questions.explain: When no validation data or fold count is supplied, AutoML cross-validates whenever training data has 20,000 rows or fewer, using three folds from 1,000 rows up and ten folds below that. At exactly 1,000 rows, that's the three-fold case, not the ten-fold one, and well under the 20,000-row threshold where a 10 percent split would instead apply.

questions.prompt: Match each hyperparameter sampling or early-termination concept to how it actually works, per Lesson 9.
right: Ends trials performing worse than the median of running averages of comparable trials
Exhaustively tries every combination, but only works with Choice (discrete) values
Supports both discrete and continuous values, and works well with early termination
Picks each new trial's values based on how earlier trials performed
questions.explain: Random sampling supports discrete and continuous values and pairs well with early termination — usually the first pass. Grid sampling is exhaustive but only works with Choice values. Bayesian sampling picks each new trial using the results of earlier ones. Median stopping ends trials that fall below the median of running averages of comparable trials.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a two-step Azure ML pipeline (data prep then train) in the correct order, per Lesson 10.
items: data_prep's script reads the raw data input and splits it into train and test folders
data_prep writes its train_data and test_data as declared component outputs
train_model receives data_prep's train_data and test_data outputs as its own inputs
train_model fits the model and writes it to its own declared model output
questions.explain: data_prep first reads and splits the raw data, then writes its results to declared outputs. The pipeline wiring connects those outputs to train_model's inputs, and only then does train_model fit the model and write its own output — exactly how `p.outputs.train_data` feeding into `train_model(...)` connects the graph in the SDK.

questions.prompt: A sweep job's base command declares a search space with Uniform(min_value=0.01, max_value=0.9) and sets primary_metric="accuracy". Select every true statement about what actually makes this sweep work, per Lesson 9.
options: The training script must log a metric named exactly "accuracy" with mlflow.log_metric, or the sweep has nothing to optimize
max_concurrent_trials can exceed what the compute cluster can actually run at once, and Azure ML will still run them all simultaneously
Each trial re-runs the entire script from scratch, including any data loading the script does
Grid sampling could be used here directly, since Uniform is a Choice-compatible distribution
Early termination policies, such as median stopping, run at every evaluation_interval, after an optional delay_evaluation
questions.explain: The objective's primary_metric name must exactly match a metric the script actually logs. Every trial restarts the whole script, including data loading — which is the trap the lesson calls out, and the reason expensive prep belongs in an earlier pipeline step instead. Early termination evaluates at each evaluation_interval after any delay_evaluation. Concurrency is capped by what the cluster can actually run, not an unlimited setting. Grid sampling only works with discrete Choice values, not a continuous Uniform distribution.

questions.prompt: On Azure Databricks, a data scientist selects the Machine Learning checkbox when creating a classic compute cluster. Per Lesson 11, what access mode does this automatically set, and why does it matter?
options: Dedicated, assigned to the user's account — Dedicated access is what lets the cluster read Unity Catalog data on an ML runtime
Shared, so multiple users can read Unity Catalog data at once from the same cluster
No Isolation Shared, which is required specifically for GPU workloads
Standard, the same access mode used by a non-ML cluster
questions.explain: Selecting the Machine Learning checkbox automatically sets the access mode to Dedicated, assigned to the user's account, and Dedicated access is exactly what lets the cluster read Unity Catalog data on an ML runtime.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about registering and promoting models in Databricks' Unity Catalog, per Lesson 12.
options: A registered model's full name has three levels: catalog.schema.model
Unity Catalog supports the older MLflow registry stages (Staging, Production, Archived) the same way a plain MLflow server does
An alias like Champion can be re-pointed from one model version to another without changing the code that loads models:/<name>@Champion
Creating a registered model in Unity Catalog needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and CREATE MODEL privileges on the enclosing objects
A new model version registered in Unity Catalog does not need a signature, as long as an input_example was logged for a previous version
questions.explain: Unity Catalog model names are three-level (catalog.schema.model), registering needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and CREATE MODEL privileges, and re-pointing an alias like Champion lets a batch job pick up a new version on its next run without any code change. Unity Catalog does not support the older registry stages — aliases are used instead. Every new version must carry its own signature; it isn't inherited from an earlier version's input_example.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: to give each training example the feature snapshot that actually existed at its own timestamp, rather than a later one, Lesson 13 uses pandas' ________ function to match each event to the most recent snapshot at or before its own timestamp.
questions.explain: pandas.merge_asof performs exactly this point-in-time join: for each event, it finds the most recent snapshot row at or before that event's timestamp, which is how the lesson prevents a later snapshot from leaking into an earlier training example.

questions.prompt: A Spark DataFrame is scored in Microsoft Fabric using the PREDICT feature's MLFlowTransformer. Per Lesson 14, what must the registered MLflow model satisfy before PREDICT can score it?
options: It must be in MLflow format with its signature populated, describing the input columns and what the model actually returns
It must be registered with mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc") specifically, even inside Fabric
It must be a deep learning model, since PREDICT does not support the scikit-learn or XGBoost flavors
It must accept multi-tensor inputs, since PREDICT is designed around tensor-shaped data
questions.explain: PREDICT's documented requirement is that the model be in MLflow format with a populated signature describing the input columns and what it actually returns. It explicitly supports flavors including sklearn, XGBoost and LightGBM, and explicitly does not support multi-tensor inputs or outputs — the opposite of options C and D.

questions.prompt: Match each of the three Microsoft ML platforms covered so far to how it names and organizes a registered model.
right: A name plus an incrementing version number, with mutable tags like stage=Prod as the documented promotion convention, and no @alias support
A three-level catalog.schema.model name, with an @alias such as @Champion used to mark deployment status instead of stages
An ML model workspace item created from a run, where each registration adds a version, and PREDICT requires a populated signature
questions.explain: Azure ML registers a model under a name with an incrementing version, using tags such as stage=Prod as the promotion convention, since it has no alias support. Databricks' Unity Catalog uses a three-level catalog.schema.model name and aliases instead of the older stages. Fabric's ML model item gets a new version per registration, and its PREDICT batch-scoring feature requires a populated signature.

questions.prompt: A deployed churn model needs to move from version 1 to version 2 without breaking any application that already calls it. Which statement correctly describes how Azure ML's online endpoint/deployment split makes that possible?
options: The endpoint is the stable name and auth mode that callers use; deployments behind it hold the model, scoring script, environment and compute, so a new deployment can be added and traffic shifted to it without changing what callers point at
The endpoint holds the model file directly, so upgrading means editing the endpoint's model property in place
Each deployment has its own unique endpoint name, so callers must update their URL whenever the model changes
An online endpoint can only ever have one deployment at a time, so the old deployment must be deleted before a new one can be created
Blue/green rollout requires deleting the endpoint and recreating it under the same name for every new model version
Traffic percentages can only be set to 0 or 100 for any single deployment; partial splits between deployments are not supported
questions.explain: The endpoint is a stable name and authentication mode; the model, scoring script, environment and compute all live on a deployment behind it. Keeping that split is exactly what lets a team add a second deployment (green), test it, shift traffic gradually, and retire the old one — all without callers ever changing what they point at.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B puts the model on the endpoint itself, but the model actually lives on a deployment, not the endpoint. That separation is the entire point of the design — it's what keeps the endpoint's interface stable while the deployment underneath it changes.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to change a registered model version's underlying files to point at a newly retrained artifact, while keeping the same name and version number. Per Lesson 15, can they do that?
options: No — only description and tags can be updated on an existing model version; any change to the files requires registering a new version
Yes, as long as the new file is the same size in bytes as the old one
Yes, but only if the model's type is custom_model rather than mlflow_model
No — once registered, a model version's tags cannot be changed either
questions.explain: The docs are specific that for a registered model, only description and tags can be updated — everything else, including the underlying files, is immutable. A change to the files means registering a new version, which is exactly why the registry increments version numbers rather than overwriting in place.

questions.prompt: A scoring script for a real-time endpoint defines init() and run(raw_data). Select every true statement about this contract, per Lesson 16.
options: init() runs once when the container starts, and is where the model should be loaded
run() is called on every request and receives the request body as a string that the script must parse itself
AZUREML_MODEL_DIR is an environment variable that points at the model folder during deployment
If run() raises an unhandled exception, the client automatically receives the exact Python traceback in the response body
Testing the scoring script locally requires Docker, since the Azure ML inference HTTP server only runs inside a container
questions.explain: init() loads the model once at container startup; run() is called per request and must parse the raw request body itself; AZUREML_MODEL_DIR points at the model folder. A client that triggers an error in run() sees only a generic 500 message — the real traceback (such as a KeyError) only appears in the server log, not the response. The Azure ML inference HTTP server is specifically a way to test a scoring script without Docker.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 18 calls the case where the distribution of a model's inputs changes over time ________ drift, distinguishing it from prediction drift, where the model's outputs change instead.
questions.explain: Data drift is the term for the model's inputs shifting in distribution — for example, customers now spending more per month than the ones the model trained on. Prediction drift is the companion term for the outputs shifting instead.

questions.prompt: Match each Azure ML model-monitoring signal to what it actually measures, per Lesson 18.
right: Changes in which features matter most to the model's predictions (in preview at time of writing)
Null rate, data type error rate, and out-of-bounds rate in incoming data
The distribution of the model's outputs changing over time
The distribution of the model's inputs changing relative to a reference baseline
questions.explain: Data drift measures the model's inputs shifting relative to a reference baseline. Prediction drift measures the model's outputs shifting. Data quality tracks null rate, type-error rate and out-of-bounds rate. Feature attribution drift tracks shifts in which features drive predictions, and was in preview at the time the lesson was written.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a blue/green safe rollout for a new model version in the correct order, per Lesson 16.
items: Add a second deployment, green, behind the existing endpoint, with zero traffic assigned
Test green directly by naming it in invoke, without affecting live callers
Mirror a percentage of live traffic to green while callers still receive blue's answers, and compare metrics and logs
Shift live traffic gradually, e.g. endpoint.traffic = {"blue": 90, "green": 10}
Send all traffic to green and delete the blue deployment
questions.explain: Safe rollout adds green at zero traffic first, tests it directly without touching live callers, mirrors a slice of real traffic to it while blue still answers callers, then gradually shifts real traffic, and only at the end cuts over fully and removes the old deployment — never editing blue in place along the way.

questions.prompt: A data scientist removes the sensitive 'group' column from training data entirely, trains a model, and finds similar overall accuracy across groups A and B. Per Lesson 19's fairness experiment, what does this actually demonstrate?
options: Similar accuracy can hide a large gap in selection rate and recall by group, because the model can reconstruct the excluded attribute from features that correlate with it
Removing the sensitive column guarantees the model cannot discriminate by group, since it never sees the attribute directly
Fairlearn's MetricFrame cannot be used once the sensitive column has been removed from training
Demographic parity difference is undefined whenever the sensitive attribute is excluded from the model
questions.explain: In Lesson 19's experiment, accuracy looked similar across groups (0.869 vs 0.852), but the model approved 58% of group A versus only 37% of group B, and found 88% of A's true positives versus 82% of B's. The model never saw the group column, yet reconstructed the pattern from correlated features — exactly why 'fairness through unawareness' fails and why outcomes must be measured by group, not inferred from excluding a column.

questions.prompt: A DummyClassifier using strategy="most_frequent" is evaluated on the capstone's churn data (35% churn rate) and scores 0.647 accuracy, an AUC of 0.5, and 0.0 recall. Why is building this baseline worth doing before training a real model, per Lesson 20?
options: It shows accuracy alone is a poor headline metric here — a model that predicts nobody churns still looks 65% 'accurate' while catching zero churners, so the real model must be judged on AUC and recall, not accuracy
It proves the dataset is too imbalanced for any model to ever beat an AUC of 0.5
It establishes the exact accuracy any production model must exceed, with no attention paid to AUC or recall
It shows that DummyClassifier is unusable for binary classification tasks in scikit-learn
questions.explain: The dummy baseline looks deceptively decent on accuracy (0.647) while finding zero churners at all — an AUC of exactly 0.5 and 0.0 recall. That's the whole lesson: with a 35% churn rate, accuracy alone would reward a useless model, which is why the real pipeline is judged against AUC (0.75 target) and recall, not accuracy.

questions.prompt: Lesson 22's segment-by-contract-type check found AUC fairly steady (0.758 / 0.729 / 0.796) but recall at a 0.5 threshold of 0.604 / 0.272 / 0.147 for month-to-month, one-year and two-year customers respectively. Select every true statement about this finding.
options: A single global probability threshold of 0.5 fits the three segments very differently, because each segment has a different underlying churn rate
Because AUC is steady across segments, the model ranks customers reasonably well everywhere, even though the fixed threshold catches very different fractions of churners per segment
Lowering each segment's threshold to match its own churn rate raised recall in all three segments with no change in precision
This weakness would have been invisible if the only metric reported were overall AUC across all customers combined
The weakness was caused by a data leakage bug in the training script, which the lesson then fixed
questions.explain: The segments have churn rates of 46%, 27% and 14%, so one fixed 0.5 threshold catches very different fractions of each, even though AUC (how well the model ranks customers) stays fairly steady. Reporting only overall AUC would have hidden this entirely. Using a per-segment threshold equal to each segment's own churn rate did raise recall (0.67 / 0.73 / 0.77), but precision fell in every segment (0.66 / 0.43 / 0.25) — a real trade-off, not a free fix. Nothing in the lesson attributes this to a leakage bug; it's a threshold/calibration issue.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: to stop a managed online endpoint from billing once you're finished with it, the capstone's cleanup checklist calls ml_client.online_endpoints.________(name="churn-endpoint").
questions.explain: ml_client.online_endpoints.begin_delete(name=...) removes the endpoint and all its deployments. A managed endpoint keeps compute allocated for as long as it exists, so the cleanup checklist treats deleting it as a required step, not an optional one.

questions.prompt: Put these six stages of the capstone's architecture in the correct order, per Lesson 20.
items: Data and baseline: build the dataset and a dumb baseline the real model must beat
Train and track: compare several candidate models with MLflow
Register: save the best model as a named, versioned asset in the workspace
Deploy: put the registered model behind a real-time endpoint, and optionally a batch endpoint
Monitor: set up data-drift signals and alerts
Review and present: check fairness and segments, write the model card, clean up, and present
questions.explain: The capstone follows the same order the whole course built toward: establish a baseline, train and track candidates, register the winner, deploy it, monitor it in production, and finally review the results honestly and present them — each stage mapping back to an earlier chapter's lesson.
